THE NEW PROGRAMME OF THE
NATIONAL EDUCATION LEAGUE.

A manifesto, embodying what may be termed
the new programme of the League, has been
issued to the representatives of tho Press in
Birmingham, for publication. The document
has been some time in preparation' and was
approved at a private meeting of the Executive
Committee, held on Thursday afternoon. It
contains an application of the principles upon
which the League was founded to the exi-
gencies of the Education question in England
at the present time.
The report of the meeting is the following :
,
NATIONAL EDUCATION LEAGUE.

, -
A meeting of the Executive 'Committee was
held at the offices, Ann-street, Birmingham,
on Thursday, Ml'. Joseph Chamberlain in the
chair. The usual reports from the officers and
committees were presented. Resolutions were
adopted urging the branches to petition in
favour of Mr. Dixon's resolutions to be proposed
early in the session, and it was reported that
in many parts of the country strong represen-
tations had been made to members of Parlia-
ment on the subject. In accordance with re-
quests from leading members of the League,
the Executive took into consideration the posi-
tion of the Eduontimi question, as affected by
the working of the Education Act, the increase
of building grants for denominational schools,
the increase of the annual grant, and the
demands of the Irish Roman Catholic prelates
for a sectarian system of education. After
mature consideration the following recommen-
dations were adopted by the Executive Com-
mittee as indicating the manner in which the
yrinciples of the League are applicable to the
circumstances thus created :

1. The compulsory election of School Boards
in all districts.

2. No schools to be recognised as Podia.-
'century schools but those under the control of
elected. School Boards.

3. Existing schools to be used during hours
of secular instruction, to be given under the
direction ot School Boards. The buildings to
be retained for all other purposes by the
denomination with which they are connected.
4. Any school, in respect to which such con-
trol is declined, to be excluded from partici-
pating in the annual Government grant.

5. In all schools provided by School Boards,
entirely separate and distinct from the time
allotted to ordinary school teaching, rooms
may be set apart for instruction in religion on
week7days. Such religious instruction to be
given by denominations at their own cost, and
by their own teachers appointed. No advan-
tages to be given to one denomination over
another. In case of dispute, appeal to be made
to the Education Department.

LONDON.

THE LONDON comroarrom AND THE NINE HOURS

MOVEMENT.

A circular has just been sent to the master
printers of London, signed by Mr. It. Lee, chair-
man, and Mr. H. Self, secretary of the London
Society of Compositors, in which the following
propositions are made :-
1. That the master printers of London be
memorialised for a reduction of the hours of labou
to 54 per week.
2. That overtime shall commence after 7 p.m.
from Monday to Friday, and after 2 p.m. on
Saturday, each day standing on its own merits.
3. That an advance of Id. per 1,000 on all
descriptions of composition (newspapers excepted)
be conceded.

4. That the above alterations shall come into
operation on all works put in hand on and after
the Ist of March, 1872.
The circular concludes—

Owing to the non-existence of any Association
representing the master printers of London, we
are compelled to apply to you, in the first instance,
personally; but if you think it preferable that a com-
mittee should be appointed to act on your behalf in
the settlement of the question, we shall be quite
ready to fall in with such a view, and hold our-
selves prepared to meet your representatives on an
early day.

articles.title: AMALGAMATED CARPEXTEES.
articles.text:
THE AMALGAMATED CARPEXTEES.

In the monthly report just issued by the Coun-
cil at Whitefriars-street, London, the General
Secretary, Mr. Harry, makes the; following re-
marks on Registration :
" In the November Monthly Report, we:drow
your attention to the conduct of our opponents, in
reference to the question of Registration; and we
also stated that with the documents in our posses-
sion, sent us on the subject by Mr. Bruce, the
Home Secretary, and the information obtained
from certain Members of Parliament, we were'
calmly and confidently awaiting the result.
"We are now in a position to state that Mr.
Bruce has issued the Regulations by which the
Registrar is not allowed to register a Trades Union
under a name identical with that of any other
existing Trade Union known to him, whether re-
gistered or not registered, or so nearly resembling
such name as to be likely to deceive the members
or the public.
"And further, that upon an application for the
registration of a Trade Union, which is already
in operation, the Registrar, if he has reason to
believe that the applicants have not been duly
authorised by such Trade Union to make the same,
may, for the purpose of ascertaining the fact, re-
quire from the applicants such evidence as may
seem to him necessary. Thus it will be seen that
the Registrar must have evidence that no other
Trade Union exists as such bearing our title, and
that evidence we can immediately furnish when
called upon, inasmuch as the E.C. and G.S. were
duly elected, according to rule, and that the E.C.,
in virtue of being the General Trustees for the
entire body, removed from the late G. 0., and still
retains all the property, documents, and records a
the Society. The E.C. does not recognise the
existence of any other Trade Union bearing our
name, but simply regard those Branches who have
violated the Rules as having seceded from the
Society. The E.C., having never once doubted the
legality of their position and conduct, are patiently
waiting for the final issue. In all probability, be-
fore wo again address you the whole question will
have assumed a practical form of settlement."

articles.title: KING'S CROSS.
articles.text:
KING'S CROSS.

TIIE GREAT NOIITIIIIttN RAILWAY SERVANTS.

On Sunday night a crowded meeting of Great
Northern Railway servants was held, at the Albion
King's-cross, to take into consideration the reply of
the directors to the memorial sent them by the men
last Monday. The chair was taken by a foreman
porter, and most classes of the working servants of
the line were represented. The chairman said
most of those present knew what the reply of the
directors was. As to hours of laliour and overtime
the directors had met them half-way, and made a
concession of an hour instead of two as asked.
The shilling advance in wages, however, would
not be given to the man who were of less than
three years' service. This had produced •much
dissatisfaction among the men. Other-alterations
in the wages were made by which shunters and
under foremen would have their condition bettered,
but the head foreman thought they should get 2s.
instead of is. increase. The terms of the conces-
sions made were discussed at considerable length

and certain exceptions taken to their fairness and
justice.

The chairman ultimately put the eight proposi-
tions to the meeting seriatim, and they were
unanimously acceded to, with the exception of
the limitation of increase of pay to three years'
men, which was approved by a majority, and the
concession to the guards, which was accepted,
with a proviso that the London allowance be
agitated for. Mr. Shrives then said ho was sure ,
all who went on the deputation must have felt,
how courteously they were received by Mr.
Oakley and his colleagues, and he begged to
move "That the thanks of this meeting be
tendered to the directors of the Great Northern
Railway Company for the concessions they have
made to their servants, and to Mr. Oakley (the
general manager), Mr. Ashley (the goods manager),
and Mr. Agard (the goods superintendent), for the
manner in which they considered and supported
the representations of the men." A porter
seconded the resolution, which was carried amidst
loud cheering. A vete of thanks to the chairman '
and the committee closed the proceedings, which
were admirably conducted from first to last.

THE IRON WORKERS' STRIKE.

The ironmasters of Keigbley, in Yorkshire, who
have more than 2,000 persons in their employment,
have made another proposition to the turn-outs,
involving the reference of a dispute as to " the
inquiry vote, overtime, and notice" to arbitration.
At a rather stormy meeting on Thursday evening
last, the proposition of the masters was ultimately
accepted on a formal resolution. The committee
representing the men conveyed the result in,
writing to the employers, but they appended,
some other conditions as to the mode of effecting
the object that induced the employers' committee
again to demur, and unless some modification or
the terms of the racn's committee can be effected
there is no immediate prospect of the strike being
brought to an end. Some persons have not ceased
work during the strike. A letterhas been received
by a workman named Thomas Larkin, in the
employ of Messrs. Summerseales. It ordered him
to cease work within five hours of his receiving
the letter, and not to resume it so long as the
"ticket of leave" was in existence, at the setae
time threatening that if he did not. he might make
his grave in the yard when he liked. The letter
was shown to the police, and a placard has been
issued offering a reward for the apprehension of the
writer. The placard sets forth that the letter was
written in a feigned handwriting, and was
evidently the work of some one not accustonie I to
writing.

BIRMINGHAM.
THE -NUT AND BOLT ronGEns.

The nut and bolt forgers in the Birrningbacl

to the adoption of a list of prices by tho menu'

propose to deduct from the workmen's wages
"threepence per hour for every hour the men lose

blast where the fair blast is used, and 68.
per week for carrying breezes." The masters
have consented to reduce the horn's of labour to
54 per week, but as the men say that when the
hours were 60 pc'r week they could not then obtain

a livelihood, they consider that the fewer hour
and a reduction of one-tenth upon their wages will
make their position, altogether insupportable. The
manufacturers have published notices, in which
they insist as a condition of the men commencing
work that they shall individually subscribe to the
rules of the Manufacturers' Insolation, and with-
draw from the Nut and Bolt Makers' Protection
Society, or any other society or union ef such
Operatives.

NEWCASTLE.

SUCCESS OF THE JOINERS.

After extending over nearly ten months, the
strike of joiners in Newcastle has been brought to
a termination. The demand of the men was that
the working hours should be reduced to 60 per
week, the wages continuing as before, at the rate
of 285., and these terms the employers, at a
meeting held on Friday night, determined to
concede.

Garrick-street, Wolverhampton, for the purpose of
considering the advisability of making application

A working man proposed that the:masters should

articles.title: IRON TRADE.
articles.text:
THE IRON TRADE.

On Friday there was an important conference in
Wolverhampton between the committee of the
Ironmasters' Association for South Staffordshire
and delegates chosen by the ironworkers. At a
previous similar meeting held at the close of
September, both sides averted a collision by agree-
ing upon a scale of wages which gave the men a
rise and secured it to them for nine months, the
agreement terminating next midsummer.
All the leading houses of the trade were repre-
sented in the masters, who, with the secretary,
numbered a dozen, and the workmen's representa-
tives were in the same force, the whole district
being divided into six localities, with two repre-
sentatives to each.

Mr. Barker presided, and, after a consultation,
extending, with an adjournment, over three and
a half hours, the masters submitted the following
proposition to the men
"That the standard rate of peddlers' wages
shall be based upon a scale of 10s. per ton; that
such advance or redaction of 20s. a ton in the
price of bars shall be met by an advance or reduc-
tion of ed. per ton in the price of puddling. That
minima's wages be fixed upon the proportionate
scale now existing as compared with puddlers'
wages, and shall be subjectlto an advance or
reduction of ti per cent. with such advance or
reduction of 20s. in the prieetof bare. That the rate
of puddling shall be from 10s. per ton, from and
after the first Monday in February till the end of
Juno next, and that the average price at which iron
has been sold in April, May, and June shall govern
the price for the next:six months."

The men received the proposition with much
favour. It will therefore be submitted to the
whole body of the men at meetings yet to be held,
and the decision at which they may arrive upon it
will be communicated to the Chairman of the Iron
Trade, who will thereupon take steps to convene
another similar meeting of masters and men—thus
making these representative gatherings a kind of
standing court of conciliation for the adjustment
of disputes in the iron trade of South Staffordshire
and East Worcestershire. The men's wages are
never to fall below Bs. 6d.; but they will go up
in proportion to the height of the price per ton of
bars. Further, the mon get 6d. a ton advance
during five of the nine months over which their
agreement to accept 6d. less, extended.

. STAFFORDSHIRE.
TON WAGlis AGITATION AMONG COLLTERS.

The agitation in the Black Country collieries,
which for six weeks has been impending, came to
a head on Saturday. The magnitude of the move-
ment may be inferred from the fact :that about
12,000 men and 25,000 women and children, be-
sides the whole trade of a large district, wore con-
cerned.

Seven years ago a disastrous strike in the same
district lasted several months, and attracted
general attention all over England. 'rho present
agitation began about five weeks ago, and was
directed to a shortening of the day's work from
eleven to nine hours.

After several conferences among masters and
men, notices were tendered and expired, some of
them on the 13th, and most of them on Saturday.
Last week a large body of men left work
before their notices expired, and the result was
that about thirty men were summoned to the
police-courts. They were, however, discharged
by arrangement, and at a meeting of the masters
on Friday night the employers agreed to reduce
the hours to 58 per week, namely, Monday six to
four, with a dinner hour, Tuesday, Wednesday,
Thursday, and Friday six to five, with a dinner
hour, and Saturday six to four, with dinner hour.
The employers decided to raise coal one shilling
per ton.

The terms thus offered were accepted by a large
representative meeting of miners held on Satur-
day night, and the colliers resumed their work on
Monday, having gained the reduction of hours
from 06 to 58 per week.

TIMISDAY.—Tho colliers have carried out the
intention declared by them last week, and notices
have been served, en mane, on the colliery owners
of the entire district, the requirements being that
henceforward the day in the pit shall not exceed
nine hours, and that of this one hour shall be for
dinner, thus reducing tho working hours to eight,
except on Saturday, when it is to be six hours.
The men will be supported by the Amalgamated
Association of Miners. The notice will expire the
week after r ext.

stated their case, and said that whilst some of the

BRADFORD.

THE PACTOILY ACTS.

On Saturday afternoon Mr. Alia% M.P. (who
has visited Bradford for the purpose of attending
a public meeting in favour of the Ballot Bill and
electoral reform), met a deputation in that town on
the subject of obtaining legislative provisions for
further restricting the hours of labour in factories.
The recent movement for the adoption of the nine
hours system haa led to the formation of an
asaociation in the manufacturing districts for the
purpose of seeking to effect such an amendment
of the Factory Act as will reduce the hours of
labour in factories from 60 to 64 hours per week
BO far as children and women are concerned, The
object of the deputation, which included Mr.
Joseph White and Mr. M. Balme, was to assertain,
on behalf of the association, how far Mr. Miall
might be disposed to support such a measure when
it came before the House of Commons. After
several members of the deputation had spoken in
explanation and exposition of the association's
object, Mr. Miall replied that he entirely sympa-
thised with the object in view. If there were any
difference of opinion it would be only with regard
to the means of arriving at that object. The ease
was a strong one, and if he could bring his judg-
ment into entire concurrence with his sympathies
he would be glad indeed to give it his support.
But he would like time for consideration, and he
would let them know his decision. Ho would be
assisted in his consideration if ho were not expect-
ed to snake any communication till he had seen the
Bill. He would see Mr. Mundella on the subject
and ascertain his intentions, and would not keep
the association in doubt as to his opinion any
longer than necessary. The deputation expressed
themselves satisfied, and thanked the hon. member
for his courtesy in admitting the interview.

WORKING MEN'S ,COMMITTEE
FOR PROMOTING TILE

SEPARATION OF CHURCH AND STATE.

TO THE WORKING CLASSES OP GREAT BRITAIN.

FELLOW WORKMEN,—
The Working Men's Committee has been formed
in consequence of a prevalent impression that
the time is come when the question of Separa-
tion of Church and State must be referred to the
final judgment of the people. In the last Session
of Parliament, it was submitted by Mr. Miall to
the judgment of the Rouse of Commons. In
doing this, he had no expectation of immediate
success. As, however, an Act of Parliament had
separated the Church from the State in Ireland, ho
felt himself warranted in asking the Legislature to
apply the principle of that measure to the rest of
the United Kingdom. lie was met with the objec-
tion that the case of Ireland was peculiar—which
indeed it was circumstantially, but not substan-
tially. Nevertheless, the Government which had
undertaken the disendowment and dieestablishment
of the State-Church in Ireland, did not oppose the
motion upon its merits, but attempted to show that
the question was uot yet ripe for legislative action.
Mr. Gladstone closed his speech by suggesting to
Mr. Miall, that ho must first convince a majority
of the people of the wisdom and justice of his
policy, before expecting Parliament to adopt it.,
This unequivocal challenge of the Premier has
been accepted ; and the Society for the Liberation
of Religion freom State-Patronage and Control has
determined to, appeal to the people for an expres-
sion of opinion on the subject. The Working Men
of Great Britain have tinier yet, as a body, pro-
nounced any judgment on this great question; but
it has been felt that, after thehroad challenge thrown
down by the Premier, they can no longer, with
respect either to,hiaa er to themselves, refrain front
a declaration of their honest and deliberate senti-
ments, From Mr. Mill, and the great party,that
lie has fornied in the countrY, Mr. Gladstone, as
loader of the Liberal party in the Itouso of Com-
mons, and also as first Minister of the Crown, has,
in set terms, appealed to the People. It behoves
Working Mon, therefore, to answer that appeal;
and that, not simply upon the purely numerical
ground suggested by Mr. Gladstone, as to whether,
among the adult population of this Island, the
majority are in favour of, or against, the Die-
endowment and Disestablislnuent of the State-
Church in Britain, as in Ireland; but also,
and perhaps especially, with a view to the
return of pledged candidates at the next
General Election, Whensoever that may take
place. The House of Commons, as now consti-
tuted, does not embody a faithful and, com-
plete representation of the whole people; and,
without taking a poll of the .whole population, the
only moans of answering the challenge of the Pre-
mier consists.in the election of a House of Commons,
each member of which has been returned" with a
special view to. his avowed, opinion on the great
question thus gravely put to the 3111110.
These, then, are the circumstances under which
the Working Men's Committee for promoting th
Separation of Church and State has been formed,
and now proceeds to Work. '

The views of the Committee may be thus eon-
sisely stated—

1. They rogard matters of religion RS belonging
to the domain of conscience, in which everything
must be left between man and his Maker.

2. They are of opinion that, since the State
Church in one part of the United Kingdom has
been diseatabliahed,it is both unjust and incon-
sistent not to deal in a similar manner with the
State-Churches of the other parts of the United
Kingdom

3. They are persuaded from observation and
experience, that the State-Church has utterly
failed to accomplish the teak for 'which it was
established; and are also convinced that its
existence, as such, is a fatal hindrance to the
attainment of those objects whieh ehurches of any
kind profess to keep in view. •
4. The State-Church of England has failed as
manifestly as the State-Church in Ireland; the
only difference being, that, while the bulk of the
Irish People were Roman Catholics, in contradis-
tinction to the avowed Prnteutantism of the then
State-Church, the great majority of the British
People are either members of the different Pro-
testant Nonconformist Churches, or of the Church
of Rome, or are willing to remain of no Church,
rather than attach themselvea to the Establish-
ment.

6. The immense revenues of the English. and
Scottish Establishments alone constitute a great
argument against their continuance; hecatu•e
these revenues, though the common property
of the whole nation, are distributed among the
religious teachers of half, or less than half, of the
people. Enormous and diipraportionate salaries

JAN. 27, 1872_._

and emoluments are paid to Bishops and other
Dignitaries, while, of that portion of the fund
which is received by the parochial clergy, by far
the largest part falls to those who have the fewest
parishioners, and the smallest to such as minister
among the densest populations.
6. The obstructiveness of the Establishment is
an additional reason for abolishing it. Its bishops
and clergy are neither appointed nor controlled by,
nor are they responsible to, the People. Jealous
of their own privileges, they resist all clang"
which may affect their own ascendancy, or that of
the Establishment in which they have- so strong a ,
vested interest. Hence, in every agitation of a
political or social character, they are always on
one side and the People on the other.
7. The Establishment is a source of national
weakness, because it divides the nation into two
hostile parties. It prevents good men uniting, as
they otherwise might unite, in works of philan-
thropy and in movements for social reform. It
thus careless mischievous sectarianism into almost
all the affairs of life.

Such are the questions which the Committee of
Working Men commend to the serious consideration
of their fellow workmen throughout the country.
In order to ascertain and give effect to their views,
Branch Committees will be formed, and meetings
held, in all the large towns. It is hoped, and 'believed,
that the practical result will be that, after this
great question has been submitted to the electors,
when it is next debated in the House of Cormnons,
Mr. Mall will be in a position to give to Arr.
Gladstone's challenge a satisfactory and decisive
answer.—WO are, on behalf of the orkiflg

, To. the Editor of•the
Sin,—The proposition Cost the Limit of
Price----so simple., so seemingly unimportant,
and yet so • obviously true, when properly
apprehended, so perfectly consonant with
the natural sentiment of right in es;ory mind,
will appear by -RS results to be a most radical
proposition. A rigid adhesion to it in com-

.every species of traniaction among men:' It
will, however; do to beneficently for all.
• The first grand consequence resulting from
this simple principle of Equity, is that what-
ever we possess which !moos/ no human labour,
-which has imposed no burden in its production,
which has cost nothing, although it is suscep-
tible of being property, is, nevertheless, not
a .right/ill subject of • price. AU property
:of this kind, whether it is equally open to the
• enjoyment of all mankind—the property of the
rate, like air and water— or whether it
attaches more particularly to some individual,
'like genius or skill, is denominated natural
• wealth. The formula relating- to- this subleet is
that natural wealth bears no price;: thatis,
it cannot, of itself, be • made the subject of
price upon :any equitable grounds 'whatsoever,
although the resignation of so, ranch .of • it
us is required for one's own convenienne, may

• This• .prineiple. settles, siiientifleally and

:fte natnral.sttia, is neural wealiktquall3ile-
-lonffiug to all the' inhabitants' of the: earth.
It stands upoikhe• same footing, as the ocean
jandithe atmosphere. The • equitable price for
• lands upon whieli no labour has been expended
IL: zero ; for such us have been surveyed
and bounded, • or • 'cleared and fenced, Or
ploughed, cultivated- andinaproved ' • the equit-
able price in each case is the cost of as. much
-labour as rightly applied would take the same
lands in the natural state and bring them into
the state of improvement in which they are
found.
So it is withi:another natural element—
water.. Every-individual has a•right to appro-
priate so much of the common natural wealth
as is requisite to the supply of his wants. If
'ono dips up water it is no longer
natural - wealth ; it is a product -. of-his

in these cases- it: la not really the natural

Simple equity Cuts up by the roots :all.apecu-

ono species of natural wealth. !It is not like
air and water, equally distributed by nature

joyment of it, in the fact of its .possession,
Whieli cannot be participated with others. It
• is the- same -with health or personal beauty
or a natural graceful deportment. In this

• •. It follows that neither the female • talents,

THE WEEK'S NEWS.

A. meeting of Volunteer Commanding
Officers was held on Saturday, at the rooms of
the National Rifle Assooiation, when resolu-
tions were, passed recognising the value of the
Easter Monday field-days, and by a large
majority Arighten •was selected as the place
for this year s.gathering.

A meeting of the magistrates of' the county
of Cork was .held on, Saturday, Lord l'ernioy
presiding, at which ,a loyal address to the
Queen and the Princess of Wales upon the
recovery of the Ileir•Apparent was adopted
unanimously.

The Worcestershire Chamber of Agricul-
ture have passed a resolution expressing their
opinion that " a moderate and equitable system
of tenant-right" should. be established in this
country.

Should the working men of Finsbury no-
minate a candidate for the seat on the London
15ehool Board, which will be rendered vacant
on the retirement of Mr. M'Cullagh Torrens,
M.P., the Labour Representation League have
resolved to support such candidate to the best
of its ability.

During the prevalence of a dense fog on
Saturday night two railway accidents occurred.
ot Newark, but, although several passengers
were shaken and bruised, there,was no loss of
life.

• Lord Penzance, Mr. Justice Mellor, and
Mr. ,Tustice Brett, sitting is the full Court of
Divorce, on Saturday refused, an application
for a new trial in the Firebraoe case, which
was heard at ouch length a few weeks ago.

the case of a son of the late General Mundy
We before Mr. Registrar Spring Rico. One of
the creditors was a West-end iterist, and

moss rose, and ten guineas for some lilies of
the valley, The unsecured debts were £5,811,
and the secured debts £10,320. The bank-
rupt passed his oxatninatiou. ,

about ThU members,, thereupon proceeded to
M. Thiers, at, his official residence, and laid
this resoluti94, before him. M. Thiers seid he
was greatly flattered by the expression of con-

fully intended to retire, being weary and dis-

Ojioiel. the Courts.martial, which have been

One hundred and twenty vestrymen of the
parish of St. Leonard, Shorediteh, were on
Tuesday summoned at the Worship-street
Police-court to show cause why they had neg-
lected to comply with an order of the
guardians to pay three separate sums of
£4,soo,each, the same being required for the
maintenance of the poor. The vestry had
refused payment in the absence of what they
considered proper and detailed accounts of the
parochial expenditure. On the part of the
defendants an objection was taken to the form
of the summons, for it was contended that the
vestry were a corporate body, and ought to
have been proceeded against through their
clerk. After a long discussion the summonses
wore withdrawn without costs.

On Tuesday, at the Wandiworth
Police-
court, a licensed victualler, carrying on
business in Clapham, wastined in the mitigated
peaalty of £5, for hawking beer in the streets,
and selling to persons who had not previously
ordered it.

The Bishop of Gloucester and Bristol, in
addressing a meeting of the Church Defence
Association on Tuesday, said the time had
arrived for the Church to assume an attitude
of defence. The Nonconformists had avowed
their resolution to contend. no longer for
toleration, nor even for equality, but for some-
thing very like supremacy. It was impossible
to resist the convietion that a session of de-
termined aggression was corning on. Thus
there arose the bitter nseessity—a necessity
to be deprecated. beyond all words—of the
Church of England standing on her defence.

The Rev. G. W. Conder lectured at Stratford
on Monday night on the national aspects of the
Establishment question, and was followed by
,the Rev. Thomas Scott, Vicar .of West Ham,
who defended the Establishment for the work
it was doing and the superiority of its ma-
chinery over that of the Nonconformist
Churches. Mr. Scott was replied to by Mr.
Condor aud by Rev. J. Knaggs; but the spec-
tacle of a clergyman calmly disonising dis-
establishment with Dissenters was felt to be a
remarkable sign of the times. At the seeend
of the lectures, on politics, nett Monday, the
subject will. be "Licensing Reform," and. Mr.
W. R. Selway. and, Mr. Andrew Johnston,
M.P., will speak.

supporters in the Houle of Commons, remind-
ing them that Parliament will moot on Tues-
day, February 6, when, immediately after
the business connected with the Address, the
Speaker will retire from the chair, "which he
has occupied so long, and with so much
honour.' The House will then be invited to
proceed to the election of a successor, and the
Premier expresses .a hopo that it may meet
the convenience of the Liberal members to be
present both at the moving of the Address
and at the election of the new Speaker.

night distributed tho prizes and, certificates

evening at the Chambers of Sir Antonio Brady,
it WAS resolved to begin a movement for esta-
blishing a university for the spread of tech-
nical education amongst the industrial classes..

The nomination for the northern division of
the West Riding has been fixed for February
3, and the election is to take place on the 6th,
the date ,of the meeting of Parliament, Mr.
Isaac Holden, and, Mr. F, S. Powell, who
formerly represented. Kuaresborough and Cam-
bridge respectively, the one as a Liberal and
the other as a Conservative, are the only
candidates before the electors. There has
been no contest in this division since it was
created, an independent constituency. in 1861.

An inquiry was on Monday opened into
the circumstances attending the death of the
man Sargent, who was killed at an explosion
which took place in a cartridge factory a few
clays ago. Only two 'witnesses had, however,
been called when the inquest was adjourned
omequeuoe of the illness of a juryman. i

A Dutch sailor belonging to a Rotterdam
steamer was on Tuesday convicted at the
Mansion-house of smuggling. He was fined
£lOO, with the alternative of six months'
imprisonment with hard labour.

According to the Paris Temps, general
satisfaction is felt, not only in Paris, but in
the provinces, at the settlement of the Parlia-
mentary conflict by the return of M. Thiers to
office. At the same time there is some little
apprehension, it admits, as to the future.
People ask if there will not be another crisis
when the financial question is again brought
forward. The Temps hopes that henceforth
M. Thiers will assume an attitude of prudent
reserve, and remember that he is no mere
Minister, or President of the Council, but an
undoubted Head of the State, placed beyond
and, above the range of Parliamentary storms.
It hopes, too, that in future he will let his
Ministers do battle for themselves in the
Assembly, and only come forward himself
upon exceptional occasions, as, for instance,
when asked by his colleagues, or when placed
in a difficult position by party combinations—
an event which the Temps thinks not likely to
occur.

opened on Tuesday, and the election of a
President took plus). Senor Herrera, the
Government candidate, baying been defeated

the election a Cabinet question, at One° com-

King.
